utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I would like to move into private session for a short while.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. On the 7th of May, the Prosecution has filed its motion for leave to amend the 65 ter summary for Witness JF-033. Now, this witness is expected to testify very soon. What the Chamber would like to know is whether the Defence, either Stanisic or Simatovic Defence, intends to respond to that motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, we were hoping that we could respond orally. Given the lateness of the Prosecution application, we haven't had the opportunity to respond in written form. We have considered the motion and we do oppose it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You do oppose it. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Likewise, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before the motion will be decided upon, an opportunity will be given for an oral response. Now, since you indicated, Mr. Jordash, that you would oppose that decision, the Chamber would like to offer some guidance in this matter. First of all, the purpose of a summary under Rule 65 ter is to provide the Defence with notice as to the facts on which each witness will testify and is given under circumstances where the content of that testimony is not yet otherwise known to the other party. I will also give some facts chronologically which may assist in better understanding the issue. On the 17th of June, 2007, the Prosecution tendered the entirety of the witness's testimony in the Milosevic case with an ex parte annex. Then on the 9th of July, 2007, both Defence teams responded, objecting to the Prosecution's motion, but they did not specifically address the 65 ter summary of Witness JF-033. On the 28th of April of 2008, two years ago, the ex parte status of the annex to the Prosecution's motion of the 17th of June, 2007, was lifted, in which the Prosecution provided a summary of the witness's evidence which indicated that the Prosecution intended to rely on the entirety of the witness's testimony in the Milosevic case. The Defence teams have not responded to this matter following the lifting of the status of the annex. Finally, the Prosecution's motion of the 7th of May, 2010, provided an amended 65 ter summary, so that the procedural record would be complete in this respect. The Chamber would like the parties to keep this in mind when responding to the motion, a motion which exclusively seeks to amend the 65 ter summary. Those are the procedural matters I would like to briefly deal with. As far as an oral response is concerned, I don't know whether we'll have time today, but if we would find time and the Chamber is thinking in terms of a response, oral response of not more than four or five minutes, would you be able to give such a response, Mr. Jordash?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If it was towards the end of the day, that would be perfectly fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we won't start with it immediately. Mr. Bakrac, same question to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will discuss it with my learned friend Mr. Jordash, and in order to save time, perhaps he will be able to articulate our position too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Then the next witness to be called will testify with voice distortion, face distortion, and pseudonym. Mr. Hoffmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, has the voice distortion been prepared? It has. Then could the witness be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness JF-038. I call you Witness JF-038 because you will testify with protective measures; that is, no one will see your face, no one will hear your voice outside this courtroom, and we'll not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- call you by your own name but by this pseudonym. Before you give evidence the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration. May I invite you to make that declaration of which the text is now handed out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, JF-038. Please be seated. Witness JF-038, you'll first be examined by Mr. Hoffmann. Mr. Hoffmann is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Hoffmann, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JF-038
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: As the Judges have mentioned, the Court has ordered certain protective measures with respect to you and your evidence here today. These include the use of a pseudonym as well as distortion of your voice and image.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And I would first ask the Court Usher to call up the pseudonym sheet on the screen, which is 65 ter 5304.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And Witness, once the document appears on the screen in front of you, I will just ask you to look at the witness name given there and the date of birth and to confirm whether that's your name and your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: JF-038
utterances.text: Yes, these are my details.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution tenders this pseudonym sheet into evidence under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P408, under seal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P408 is admitted under seal. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall giving testimony before this Tribunal on 31st March and 3 and 4 April 2006, in the Martic case?

utterances.speaker: JF-038
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And after arriving here in The Hague and in preparation for your testimony today, did you have an opportunity to review audio recordings of your testimony in that case?

utterances.speaker: JF-038
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And if you were asked the same questions today that you were asked in the Martic case, would you today give the same answers in substance?

utterances.speaker: JF-038
utterances.text: Well, I certainly would, except that since a lot of time has gone by, I may forget something, but I remember what happened. I remembered everything that occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: But when you reviewed your audio recordings, just to clarify, there was nothing incorrect when you listened to your prior testimony?

utterances.speaker: JF-038
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution at this time tenders the prior testimony of this witness. It's, in fact, three transcripts of his testimony in the Martic case. Currently they are uploaded with three different 65 ter numbers, which is 5130 to 5132. If the Chamber would prefer, we could also merge them, of course. Those should be admitted under seal in light of the protective measures and in light of the fact that the during the previous testimony some parts were given in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections? No objections. I think that all the pages are numbered and we find dates on it, so better to have them under one exhibit number. That exhibit number would be, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just need to correct the transcript for the previous one. So pseudonym sheet 5304 is not P408, under seal; it's P419, under seal. I apologise. And for these --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the same applies in relation now to P419, that it is admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And the next exhibit will be P420, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P420 is admitted into evidence and is comprised of the pages 3017 up to and including P3058, testimony dated the 31st of March, 2006; the pages 3059 up to and including 3130, that is the testimony of the 3rd of April, 2006; and pages 3131 up to and including 3176, being the testimony in the Martic case of the 4th of April, 2006. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The admission is under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, during the Martic testimony, two exhibits were admitted into evidence and the Prosecution has asked in its 92 ter motion that these be admitted into this case as related exhibits. As indicated prior to the session, the Prosecution has prepared an updated list of persons the witness has in the past referred to and may refer to today. This is now 65 ter 5303 and would replace the earlier 65 ter 2823. And the second exhibit is a chart drawn by the witness during the Martic testimony; it is 65 ter 2824. I would ask that these be, too, admitted into evidence. The list of persons should be admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objection against amending or replacing the original exhibit under 65 ter list? Yes. I got handed out just a minute before this session still a list with ERN number 0675-6632 which still bears the number 2823, not 5303. What went wrong?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: That is just a technical issue on our side. It should, in fact, refer to 65 ter 5303.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the ERN number I just read, is that the new list --

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: That is the new list that I just distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The new list with the date the 12th of May, 2010, but still with the wrong number on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Yes. We can certainly correct that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are invited to, if you change these kind of things, that you change them completely. But there are no objections. The list of names, 65 ter 5303, would be, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit P421, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P421 is admitted under seal. Just a second, please. Yes, then the chart, and there's no need to have that admitted under seal, would receive, Madam Registrar, number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 2824 becomes Exhibit P422, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P422 is admitted into evidence. I already hereby grant permission to replace the uploaded 65 ter 5303, which is admitted under seal, to have it replaced if only the 65 ter number at the bottom of the page is replaced by the accurate number, which is 5303 instead of 2823. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would ask the Court Usher to hand out a copy of Exhibit P421, that is the list of names, to the witness, so if at any time he needs to refer to one of these people, he could do so with that list on his desk. And I've provided also the same list also to the Defence prior to court. In addition, I briefly would like to call up another 65 ter exhibit, which is 65 ter 5133. It is a map from the wider Knin area. I have provided copies of that extra map to the Chamber and the Defence prior to court, and I've heard of no objections prior to court of that map being admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The map which is, by the way, a rather modern map of 2003, and, therefore, does not reflect the situation at the time, most likely, but if there are no objections, Madam Registrar, the number of this map would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P423, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P423 is admitted into evidence. The witness can keep the list and if he wants to refer to any of these persons, he can do so by referring to this list. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just one note on that list. Previously the witness indicated that the three names listed at the bottom of that page, there would be no issue naming those in public session. He is more concerned about the people that are numbered on the first part.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Witness, I will now read a short summary of your prior testimony in the interest of the public following this trial. Although it's not considered evidence in this case, I ask you to carefully listen to that summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: JF-038 was sent with a delegation of the Ministry of Interior of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the SFRY, in May 1991, to the Knin area on a mission, following an agreement between the SFRY and the Croatian republic. The group's main assignment was to calm down the tensions between the Croatian and the Serbian sides that were clashing at the time. Officially, that group were cease-fire monitors. The group consisted of members of the federal state security and the federal public security service. During the mission, the witness and his colleagues learned about the role which Milan Martic and the JNA played in the creation of the Serb autonomous region, the SAO of Krajina. The witness has described the persecution of the Croat population in the region by Milan Martic and his men. Milan Martic established a Serb police station in Knin and appointed himself commander. In addition, Martic organised the process by which the borders of the SAO Krajina were demarcated. The JNA assisted this process. First, barricades were erected, separating Serb and Croat villages. The Serb barricades were manned by police officers under Martic's control and reserve policemen that were local Serb villagers. The witness also testified to the expulsion of many hundreds of Croats from Knin by Milan Martic and his police forces in the summer of 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. We need to correct something. We cannot refer to 100.000, that's a bit of a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: There may have been a translation --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because in Knin there weren't 100.000 Croats, in Knin and the surrounding area, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. It may have been a -- either my misspelling or a translation error. What I said is, I referred to many hundreds of Croats. Not thousands. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I heard was 100.000 Croats, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whomever made the mistake, it's now corrected. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: JF-038 further testified about the presence of the accused Jovica Stanisic and the Serbian state security in the SAO Krajina. The witness also learned about the presence of Captain Dragan in Knin and the training of Knindzas at the Knin fortress, as well as the training of the Krajina police at the training centre at Golubic, near Knin. He also met with Ratko Mladic, at the time a JNA officer in Knin. JF-038 was sent on another similar mission to Eastern Slavonia and Baranja in the late summer and fall of 1991. And finally, JF-038 described the process by which the MUP of Serbia seized control of the federal MUP in Belgrade. The federal MUP was formally taken over by the MUP of Serbia on 9 October 1992. Officials of the Serbian DB took part in that take-over.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Witness, during your testimony in the Martic case, and that is on 31st March 2006, at transcript 3037 and following, you described a mission to the SAO Krajina, that there were three groups sent by the federal MUP. Each of these groups including members of the public and the state security service of the federal MUP. You testified that you were sent to troubled spots where possible conflicts would arise between Serbs and Croats; more specifically, to the areas of Gospic, Plitvice and Knin. Your own group went to the Knin area. You describe the trip to Knin in May 1991, by helicopter, during --

utterances.speaker: JF-038
utterances.text: I apologise. We did not travel by helicopter to Knin, but rather from Sibenik to Knin. To Sibenik we got by car. There was a major lapse there of some sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Witness, I was just about to come to the next topic, which is the day when you travelled by helicopter with Admiral Zec from the JNA to Knin, by helicopter, and how he was pointing at the Knin fortress and then later mentioned how the Knindzas were trained by Captain Dragan. And my question to you is, if you found out at some point later the full name of Captain Dragan? And if so, if you could give it to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JF-038
utterances.text: All of that is true. I learned about Captain Dragan much later, his real first and last names, but at this time the Admiral just mentioned this was Captain Dragan. And later on, in Belgrade, I learned that his name was Vasiljkovic, that his real last name was Vasiljkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Sir, in your prior testimony, you refer to the group of Knindzas and Arkan's men, and that is transcript 3061. My question to you, can you clarify whether these two groups or units were two distinct groups?

utterances.speaker: JF-038
utterances.text: When we flew by helicopter above the Knin fortress, Admiral Zec told us that we can see below the fortress where a certain Captain Dragan was training the Knindzas and members of the Ministry of the Interior, or rather, the Krajina police. And he also said specifically that that group comprised Knindzas, the so-called Knindzas, and some members and some units belonging to Arkan's group.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Was there any talk among you and your colleagues about generally who would be trained at Knin by Captain Dragan?

utterances.speaker: JF-038
utterances.text: Well, we did not talk about that when we were in the helicopter, but later on we exchanged views about this, us, the members of the group, who this might be and what members of what these were. We had occasion to meet these men in Knin. These were men who had some sort of black uniform, black shirts, and a bandana around their head and there was some insignia saying "Knindza" on them. As we walked in Knin, around Knin, we could see -- we could single out individuals who looked different than regular people who lived in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: At transcript page 3162, you testified in the Martic case that Captain Dragan came to the area to train special units of the SAO Krajina. Do you have any knowledge on how it was possible for Captain Dragan to come to Knin for such a training?

utterances.speaker: JF-038
utterances.text: I don't have any specific knowledge about him, but it is certain that he must have gone there by invitation. He couldn't just go there on his own, without someone inviting him. I can speculate, and there were also discussions amongst us who were in this group because to us he was a person we didn't know, so we were trying to guess who he was or who he might be and where he had come from. There were opinions, some amongst us thought that he had spent some time in Australia and that he came to the country, or rather, to Knin from Australia. But later on I also saw him in Serbia. And in view of those facts and based on my own personal knowledge and the discussions I had with the group, Legija Ulemek was brought to the service to be a leader of a special unit of the Serbian MUP. So we concluded that perhaps he too came there with someone's approval or invitation, that that's how he must have come to the country, or rather, to Knin to train the Knindzas.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: During your Martic testimony on 3 April 2006, you did testify to meetings with the Croatian side and then later on with Milan Martic to agree on a prisoner exchange. You testified that Martic referred to some detention premises in Knin, and that is at transcript 3099 [Realtime transcript read in error "1399"]. Later on, you also talked to Croats that were released during that agreed exchange, and how they reported about being detained in Knin and being mistreated during their detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: I would ask that we now see 65 ter 1916 on the screen. It is a BBC summary of a news clip from 4 April 1991 regarding a proposed prisoner exchange between the Knin police and the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hoffmann, for the record, I didn't follow you when you spoke the words, but transcript 1399 must be -- is that 3199?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: It should read transcript 3099. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 3099. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Sir, when the translation of that news clip comes up, I would ask you if you had a chance to review this BBC report prior to your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: JF-038
utterances.text: I really cannot read this nor can I see the content. It's too small. Even if I take my glasses off, it's still too small. The print is too fine, I can't read it. Now it's better.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Do you recall having reviewed this document prior to you coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: JF-038
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And although this report dates slightly before your arrival in Knin, would you say that the gist of this report with regard to the prisoner exchange between the Krajina police under Martic and the Croatian authorities is consistent with your own experience of such exchanges?

utterances.speaker: JF-038
utterances.text: Well, I can describe my own case that had to do with these exchanges, but also based on statements given by the prisoners who said that they were kept in some basement at the police station in Knin without the basic needs, sanitary conditions, and this can be interpreted to be, in fact, in correlation with what is stated here in the BBC programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution tenders this exhibit, 65 ter 1916, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit P424, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P424 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Witness, you just referred to how you were told by prisoners about their detention at the basement of the police station in Knin. Did you at any time get permission from Milan Martic to inspect any of the possible detention facilities in Knin?

utterances.speaker: JF-038
utterances.text: No, we did not. Although while the prisoners were still in detention in the prison, we asked to see them, to see where they were detained, but we weren't allowed to, and even later on we were not allowed to go and inspect those rooms, the premises. But based on the statement given by these prisoners, because we took them to Drnis in our car, according to what they said to us, those conditions were very poor. There was no sanitation of any sort. There was no room for a normal life for a prisoner. They said that they did not even have the toilet or running water, and some guards would just bring some water for them to use.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: I would ask that we see the next exhibit, 65 ter 1536, on the screen. The ERN is 0113-3713. It is a document about the prison facilities in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And, Witness, the question again, did you have a chance to review this document prior to coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: JF-038
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And can you briefly describe what this document is about?

utterances.speaker: JF-038
utterances.text: Well, there is mention there of opening some facilities in Knin where prisoners and detainees could be held, convicts, but there weren't any convicts really, rather war -- prisoners of war and providing normal conditions for them to stay there as detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Do you have any idea when this document could have been written?

utterances.speaker: JF-038
utterances.text: Well, it is possible that it was a little before our arrival. I know of these four prisoners that we managed to exchange, that was the object of our mission, but there were other detainees there because arrests were a daily occurrence. People were detained and brought in from the front line or from -- just picked up from their homes and villages, I really don't know exactly, but it was at that time, either before we arrived there or during our mission in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution tenders this exhibit into evidence. That is 65 ter 1536.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit P425, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P425 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Witness, during your Martic testimony, you also talked about the training of members of the Krajina police at Golubic, not far away from Knin. And that is at transcript 3050 on 31st March 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: I would ask that we see the next exhibit, 65 ter 1269, on the screen. It starts with ERN 0280-4583. This document is dated in Knin, 27 May 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And, Witness, the same question here, did you have a chance to review this document prior to coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: JF-038
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And if we can please go to the end of the document. I think it's on page 2 of both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And if you would be so kind just to read out who signed the document?

utterances.speaker: JF-038
utterances.text: I do not see the signature here but I see the name typed there, it says Captain Dragan Vasiljkovic, and I see also that his name was added later on, the last name. In other words, it wasn't the same typewriter that was used. It was only Captain Dragan originally, and then the name, the last name was added later on, it was typed on a different typewriter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: This document relates to the training centres and mentions the Knin fortress and the camp in Golubic. Given the date of the document and its content on the training facilities, would you say that this document in its report is consistent with your own knowledge of the mentioned topics?

utterances.speaker: JF-038
utterances.text: Yes, and this document refers to the time when we were there in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution tenders this exhibit into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we object to this document being admitted. The witness noticed himself that this document has a problem. There's a visible problem of authenticity; in other words, something was added on to the second page. We see that it was typed on two different typewriters, and also the document bears no signature, so that, in our view, the document is not authentic and we object to its being admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hoffmann, could you inform the Chamber where the document comes from.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. This document was received through one of the analysts of the Tribunal from the Croatian state archive on 7 June 2004. And if I may add on the point of whether or not the last name of Captain Dragan has been added later on, I think it's clear that with a typewriter sometimes the font is different, but even assuming that the word "Vasiljkovic" was added later, in our submission, it actually would only support that the document as such, at least without that last name, is authentic. Otherwise it would have been set up as a complete forgery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now authenticity can be challenged in two ways. First, that the whole of the document is a fraud, is a forgery; and the other one is that the document has been tampered with. Now, you say, if I understand you well, since it was not a complete fraud, the fact that it was tampered with is convincing evidence that -- I have difficulties in understanding your argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Maybe I wasn't clear. It may well have been, I don't see it that way, but I'm just taking the point for a second of the Defence, that something was added. I think the -- if we look at the addressees of the recipients of the document at the bottom of the document, they seem to appear in a similar typewriter than the last name of Vasiljkovic. So it may well have been that at the time this document was compiled, this information was added, and it's certainly the case that we got this document as we received it from the Croatian state archives. But I certainly didn't want to -- or didn't agree that it is, in fact, tampered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say, as a matter of fact, that the addressees are in this apparently put in there by the same typewriter, is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: No. All I'm saying is that it was not done with a word processor, it wasn't printed with a printer, as we are used to this these days. It was printed or typed with a typewriter, and we see at different parts of this document a different font, and this is only natural happening with a typewriter at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said: "If you look at the bottom ... they seem to appear in a similar typewriter than the last name of Vasiljkovic." So apparently your suggestion is that that was added by the same means as the name that was added.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: I apologise. I didn't mean it was typed at a later stage, but it appears to be in a similar font for whatever reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the font of a typewriter, first of all, at the time I don't know what kind of typewriter this was, but you had the ones where you could change the fonts within five minutes, the famous IBM ones, but your suggestion apparently is that the added family name is similar to the -- is typed in a way similar to the name which is not in the same typewriting as the Captain Dragan as put at the bottom of this document. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: I think we can all see that it's at least in a different font. But in the interest of time, I wouldn't insist on the admission right now if Your Honours have some doubts about the authenticity and maybe get it marked for identification and later deal with it. In our submission, it rather goes to the weight, but I certainly don't want to spend more time while the witness is present.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I add my objection and endorsement of the Simatovic team's objection. Having listened to the argument, we also submit it doesn't have sufficient indices of authenticity. The fact that there are obviously two different type fonts indicates that, at the very least, it's been made by -- on two different occasions, and given that the different type font relates to such significant information, that is, the people who are to receive the document, we submit that it ought not to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hoffmann, one of the striking elements in the typewriting, apart from the name Vasiljkovic, is that the small letter A is unusually small, that is, that it comes above the general bottom line. If you look at the word "jedan" [phoen] in the last "teksta dostavlja" you see that the A is well above what is the main bottom line for all the other letters. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, we see the same in the words "Kapetan Dragan" which therefore strongly suggests that the text typed below where there's no signature is typed with the same machine as the original. Now, it seems that in the name Vasiljkovic we have a similar feature of an A coming slightly above the general bottom line of the other letters, which at least is a first indication that all of it would have been typed perhaps by the same machine, at least with the same -- but not at the same time because apparently the intensity of the ink or the -- how clean the letters may have been was different when the word "Vasiljkovic" was typed in. So this all strongly suggests and -- but I'm not an expert in this field, that the same typewriter was used but at a different time or at least in a different circumstances, as the ink ribbon apparently not being the same. Have you inquired as to what explains this difference, which is very obvious, if you look at it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: No. There is no follow-up and I would not expect anyone in the Croatian state archives, where we got the document from, that they would be able to explain, you know, the issues of that document that they collected at some time. But, if I may add, even assuming that the last name and the recipients of that document may have been added, there may be valid -- good reasons for it that initially the document and its contents was typed up, it was handed over to some secretary and then that information was added. In our submission, this may be well an issue for the weight but not necessarily to bar the admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say if it comes to speculation, that has its effect on weight rather than on authenticity, because you are coming up with some reasons, I could invent five other reasons why, and your reasons are not per se better than mine. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just wanted to add a few more things that indicate how troublesome this document is. I'm sorry, could I just have a moment. Once again, I apologise, Your Honours. In view of the content of the text, the person that we are speaking of, Dragan Vasiljkovic, speaks Ekavian Serbian. This entire text is written in Ijkavian and that casts a completely different light on the content of the text. Also, the heading says to the secretary of the SUP. Over here we have four addressees and only the second one is the chief of SUP. Also, it is not logged anywhere, it is not registered anywhere, so all of this casts a completely different light on this document. In addition to the formal elements, could you please take into account these objections that we have in view of the way the text is written. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, whether the language used by the person who is supposed to be the author, or at least the one who signed, where they use it -- usually speaks a different dialect is a -- whether that's anything which has to do with authenticity is another matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document will be marked for identification. Madam Registrar, the number would be number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be document P426, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And keeps that status for awhile. Now, Mr. Hoffmann, you introduced this and the only question you put to the witness whether his memory corresponds with what is found here. Therefore, it seems that that document in itself, at least at this moment, has not any added value to -- apart from that this is what the witness remembers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Well, he did confirm that it's from the same time-frame that he was himself in the area when he himself saw and heard about Captain Dragan being involved in these issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then you rely on the authenticity also in respect of the date. We'll have a look at it and for the time being it's marked for identification. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Later on, Witness, during a meeting with Milan Martic in his office in Knin, Martic stated to you that the Serbs of the Krajina wanted to live in one single country with all the other Serbs from Yugoslavia including Serbia, and that is to be found at transcript 3070 on 3 April 2006. And he further stated to you and your colleagues at the time that his goal and that of the Croatia Serbs was to establish a district to unite all Serbs in Croatia, a unified state of all Serbs. And I'll play now a video-clip from 65 ter 4718. This clip runs from minute 10.52 to minute 17.14. It's an interview of Milan Martic at the Serb TV Knin on 4 July 1993. For the booth, this is actually clip number 2, and the same clip is marked in e-court as 65 ter 4718.2.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Milan Martic gave a statement for Belgrade Television which was broadcast in last night's 'Hronika srpskih krajina.' We broadcast it again now, since our viewers did not have electricity at the time."

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, I just forgot to mention one thing. We will see during part of the video that the image and the audio is distorted for a few seconds and then the interview will continue. That's just the way we received this material. I just wanted to give a warning up ahead. And would like to start the video again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have a look at it. Please restart the video.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Reporter: Exactly three years separate us, dear viewers, from the beginning of the Serbian resistance to the newly established authorities in Croatia. On the 3rd of July, 1990, Milan Martic and his comrades made it clear to Tudjman and his minister Boljkovac that they did not accept the Ustasha symbols or the new Ustasha order. Mr. Martic, how do you assess and evaluate those events now, after three years? "Martic: Well, you see, as you have said, it is three years to this day that Croatia has no authority over these areas. To decide to make such a move as we did, surely it required at least some courage. We decided to make such a move simply in order to create a turning point in history, in order for the Serbs not to rise to revolt always attacking their own gendarmerie and police, in order to prevent that. Our preparations, which took place over the year prior to the events and which hardly anyone knew about, culminated on that 3rd of July, 1990, when we presented a letter, an open letter ... and told Minister Boljkovac loudly and clearly that there is no way we were going to be part of a legislative system which would terrorise their own people. All the people knew that, and I think that that was a decisive moment in this fight of ours for survival in these areas. "Reporter: It is possible, Mr. Martic, to draw from these events a conclusion that is relevant today? Namely, you were all united at the time, both the people and the police, the Serb Democratic Party leadership and the key people in the political life of the then SAO Krajina. "Martic: Well, there are very few differences among us. We all want to have our Republic of Serbian Krajina, but there was that fanaticism. Such mutual agreement between the leadership of the Serbian Democratic Party, the officials on all positions, and us from the police, that was something equalling fanaticism. Our legendary late academician Jovan Raskovic cannot be omitted. His contribution to all of this is great. He mobilised people's spirit, our spiritual leader. I personally loved him as my own father, and to this day, I keep his picture in my office. He mobilised people's spirit and the movement started. So the Serbian Democratic Party was the movement. Milan Babic, who undoubtedly played a huge role, he was in constant communication with us and the Serbian Democratic Party, and we were worked practically along parallel lines, but absolutely along the same lines. "Reporter: In the war, as in any other war, there is crime and war profiteering and corruption. Do you manage to fight it, to deal with it? "Martic: Listen, no war, not even this war of ours, was without profiteering, corruption, and all those negative aspects. Of course, we can fight that within the limits of our capabilities as much as we can. There are certain problems. We're working on solving them, you know, certain problems, like certain dominance of war time revolutionary law and the neglect of civil law and similar, but with a strong police, we should protect the legal order, we do provide that in any case. I do not wish to enumerate now how many criminal reports we submitted and things like that. A lot has been done. However, I want that we have as little work as possible, and I endeavour that all other government structures do their job and prevent things from reaching us. Because, you know, if everyone else does their job, then there is less work for us and the legal system, in any case, functions more optimally. "Reporter: What is the situation in the theatre of war today? "Martic: Well, very favourable. You see the lines are stable, the people in that motive hold a firm belief that we should definitely have our own territory, that we should have our republic of the Serbian Krajina which we should endeavour to join with other Serbian states. Of course, these borders are fairly stable, and in this regard, all our troubles which burden us fade into the background, and by that I mean the general poverty and the difficult life in this region at the moment, but we also understand those who help us from the outside that ... that the situation is similar over there. However, the ultimate goal, to have one's own state which will be outside that infamous Croatia, outside their genocidal democracy, is of course so huge that everything else fades into the background. I am convinced that we will know how to preserve this, to preserve what we fought for and won in blood, what we liberated, and that we will definitely finalise those ultimate borders, that we will have our state which will be Serbian land, free for all goodwill citizens, but let be it known in the first place that this is our territory and not territory for some recent comers. "Reporter: Thank you Mr. Martic. "Martic: Thank you."

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise the location of this interview?

utterances.speaker: JF-038
utterances.text: Yes, it is the fort of Knin. Above the town of Knin itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And having listened to this interview of Milan Martic from July 1993, is that consistent with the way Martic expressed his goals in 1991 when you personally met him?

utterances.speaker: JF-038
utterances.text: Yes. It is practically the same speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, the Prosecution tenders this clip into evidence. It is from the same video compilation as an earlier admitted exhibit, P12, and this one is marked as 65 ter 4718.2 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: There is an objection and the objection is this: That I find it difficult to work out precisely what it is the Prosecution seek to demonstrate through this video. If it is the same speech that the witness heard, then the witness has given his evidence. If there's something else on this video that my learned friend actually wants in addition to what the witness has said, then we should hear about it, otherwise, we are simply duplicating evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let me just try to understand what the ... Mr. Hoffmann asked the witness whether what was said here in 1993 is the same as what the witness heard him saying in 1991. Of course, that would be at a different occasion and would be rather about the consistency of the aims pursued by Mr. Martic. So, therefore, I have some difficulties in understanding whether it just duplicates the evidence because it creates a time-line. Therefore, I have difficulties in understanding your argument, Mr. Jordash, before I give an opportunity to Mr. Hoffmann to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I can put my objection slightly differently. As I understood what the witness was testifying to, he testified to Mr. Martic giving a speech in 1991 which endorsed Martic's view that there should be a link between Serbian territories. I think that was the evidence. The speech that we've just heard in the video seems to have been somewhat different, which is that Martic, in 1993, was expressing a view that the ultimate goal was for the Croatian Serbs to have their own state. And then the witness confirmed somehow that the two views were the same. So my objection -- I see Mr. Hoffmann shaking his head, so perhaps I should --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are now -- we have now entered the realm of interpretation of the content rather than admissibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I withdraw the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And apart from that, of course, the witness has identified the location on which the interview took place. Mr. Hoffmann, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: I'm happy to have a break now once this clip may be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I've heard of no other objections. Madam Registrar, the clip would receive number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P426, Your Honours -- P427, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P427 is admitted into evidence. We'll have a break and we'll resume at five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hoffmann, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Witness, just prior to the break we talked about the -- how Milan Martic expressed his views and his goals about the RSK and unification with other Serbian states. My question to you is, did you at the time, that is, in the early 1990s, hear any other Serb politician make similar statements?

utterances.speaker: JF-038
utterances.text: Well, after that freedom of expression and after the multiparty system was introduced, several politicians spoke that way. First of all, it was the president of Serbia at the time, Milosevic. Then there were speeches made at different rallies; Seselj, Draskovic, as far as I can remember. Other persons too, but, well, it was this euphoria after communism and after this one-party system. People felt this need to express their own views and their own personal convictions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: So did I understand you correctly that in 1990, 1991, you did have a chance to hear any speech of Seselj as well, either live or on TV, and I'd appreciate if you'd just indicate whether yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JF-038
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: The Prosecution will play now another clip. This is from video exhibit P18, which is marked for identification. It's the BBC interview with Vojislav Seselj in March 1995. That clips runs from minute 11.33 to minute 12.48, and for the booth, this is clip 3.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "LS: Can you tell us about that moment when you realised that the Serbian people would have to take up arms to defend themselves, their freedom, and their right to remain in Yugoslavia, or to remain in a certain Serbian state? "VS: I realised that in May 1990. I happened to be in America when I heard that Tudjman had won the election, and it became clear to me that war was inevitable. As soon as I returned Belgrade, I established the Serbian Chetnik Movement because of it. One year earlier, the renowned Chetnik commander from World War II, Vojvoda Momcilo Djujic, declared me a new Serbian Chetnik Vojvoda. He was the last one alive and wanted the Chetnik tradition to be kept. Chetniks were Serbian freedom fighters from the times of the Turkish occupation, in the Balkan wars, and the First and Second World Wars. We established the Serbian Chetnik Movement but we kept repeating: 'We are ready for everything, although we would like to avoid war at all costs and resolve the situation in a peaceful manner.' We kept repeating: 'The Croats can go, but can only take those territories where they are a majority. Where they are a minority, they cannot take away the territories.'"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hoffmann, before we proceed, has the transcript under the video be verified, because there was -- I think I read in the transcript a Russian occupation, whereas it was translated by interpreters as the Turkish occupation. Now, I do not know what the original said. Perhaps I could ask the Simatovic Defence whether they have listened to the original language. Could we play that specific part again and also show the -- it was somewhere in the middle.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "VS: And then it became clear to me that war was inevitable. And as soon as I returned to Belgrade, I formed the Serbian Chetnik Movement because of it. One year earlier, the renowned Chetnik commander from World War II, Vojvoda Momcilo Djujic, declared me a new Serbian Chetnik Vojvoda. He was the last one alive and wanted the Chetnik tradition to kept. Chetniks were Serbian freedom fighters from the times of the Turkish occupation, in the Balkan wars and in the First and Second World Wars."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can stop there. Apparently there's a mistake in the -- because our interpreters now, for the second time with some emphasis, translated as the Turkish occupation whereas the transcript under it reads the Russian occupation. Let's move on, but it's now clear that there is a mistake in this material. By the way, I take it that you have listened and looked to it various times in preparing. These are important matters to notice. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And we'll certainly verify the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Witness, having listened to what Seselj expresses during that BBC interview, is that consistent with what you have heard of Seselj in 1990 or 1991?

utterances.speaker: JF-038
utterances.text: Well, as far as the portion about the unification and life of the Serbian people, yes. I mean, with minor differences to the left or right, up or down, but generally speaking, that is the essence, the gist. Depending, of course, on the situation where he held a speech, he probably adjusted, whether it was in a province or in the heart of Serbia or in some other part of the country, depending on the area where he held the speech, it would differ a little, but the objective was the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And just for the record, Your Honours may recall that the issue of that exhibit is still pending for admission in line with the submission of the Prosecution of 29 March 2010. And at this time I would just continue with my questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. Yes, my recollection is that we had portions of it played and then we put everything together? If you could assist me in refreshing my memory as to the 29th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. The parts of this interview with Vojislav Seselj had been played with various witnesses from the beginning of this trial. The Prosecution from the outset has tendered the whole video into evidence. It has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now it's clear. It was about parts and the whole of it. Then no action has to be taken, you just continue. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Well, we appreciate, of course, once the motion would be decided, but for now we can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Witness, you also testified in the Martic case that among your colleagues during the mission to the SAO Krajina, you remarked on the fact that the Serbian state security service got involved in organising the SAO Krajina state security. And that is at transcript 3078. In that context, you testified that you did see the accused Jovica Stanisic twice in the Knin area in May and June 1991. And I would ask you to briefly tell the Court where exactly did you see Stanisic in May or June 1991 in Knin?

utterances.speaker: JF-038
utterances.text: In Knin, whether it was the first time I went there or the second time, I can't remember exactly, but I did see Mr. Jovica Stanisic on one occasion with another person, person number 3, at the restaurant at Slapovi Krka, the Krka waterfalls. I remember that was in the afternoon. And the second time -- or the first time, I'm not sure which was first, we met outside the police building, outside the Knin MUP, but that was just a brief encounter in passing. We exchanged greetings. The same was true of the restaurant because he was sitting in company with some other people. We arrived there to have lunch so we just waved to each other from afar, but in Knin, outside the MUP building, we shook hands but there were no other contacts. However, I did know Mr. Stanisic from before, from Belgrade, but we did not have contact, physical contact. So even this contact in Knin was just a brief exchange of greetings. And I remember that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure whether he or I was with person number 2 on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Sir, if you can just clarify, the interpreters didn't get the last part. Could you repeat with whom you were together on that list when you saw the accused?

utterances.speaker: JF-038
utterances.text: On one occasion when I saw him I was with person number 3. That was at the restaurant. And when we met outside the police station building, the MUP building, whatever it was called then, with person number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. And just for the record, when you refer to numbers, that is from Exhibit P421. Now, Witness, according to your own knowledge at the time in 1991, what role or position did Jovica Stanisic have at that time?

utterances.speaker: JF-038
utterances.text: At that time I believe he was the acting chief of state security. Or one of the assistants. I really am not sure. Twenty years have passed and I can't be quite certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: In your Martic testimony also at transcript 3078, you refer to meetings with the Croatian security service in Sibenik, and more precisely with Branko Polizota. He told you that they had information that the Serbian service was involved in the activities in the SAO Krajina and that Serbia had organised the work of the state security on the territory of the SAO Krajina. Did you also have a chance to talk to a certain Vice Vukojevic during your mission to the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: JF-038
utterances.text: At this time Vice Vukojevic was the deputy minister of the interior of the Republic of Croatia. The first meeting, protocol meeting, was held with him, the group I was in, which was led by person under number 6, who was the leader of our group and who took us to Croatia to introduce us. And we had this meeting on the first day when we arrived in Croatia, in Sibenik, on the MUP premises. Vice Vukojevic, in that preliminary conversation, just mentioned that they were aware that the Serbian service was active or present in Croatia. He did not indicate where exactly he meant, but we took it to mean, all of us in the group, that the Croatian side never wanted to actually use the word "Serbian Krajina" or anything of that sort because it avoided using that term. But it did refer specifically to Knin and to SAO Krajina. This was the first official protocol meeting or protocol orientation. Our leader, nor any of us, decided not to go into any further discussions because that would only lead to strained relations and we felt that that would prevent us later on to actually carry out the tasks that we had, so that we avoided discussing details. But we did hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Sir, when you said he was referring to the Serbian service, how did you understand that term? As a reference to what?

utterances.speaker: JF-038
utterances.text: Vice Vukojevic said -- he only said that he was aware there was the presence of the Serbian police in Croatia, because Vice Vukojevic was a member of state security, and we members of this service would use the term "presence of the service," whereas they would say "presence of the police." So they would use the term "police presence" for this department of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Just to clarify, Witness, if you refer to "service," can you just briefly explain what service you and your colleagues were referring to?

utterances.speaker: JF-038
utterances.text: We members of state security were referring to our own service because we did not interfere in the activities of other interior services, in other words, the regular police. We just dealt with matters that pertained to our service, the state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, in 1991, did the Serbian DB, the Serbian state security, have any legal or official competence or authority to work in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JF-038
utterances.text: Under the existing laws and the rules of service the service of one republic was not permitted -- and also out of respect for our colleagues from other republics, so it was not permitted to enter the areas and conduct assignments or missions in another republic. They would always have to inform the other republic and ask for their approval if it was necessary for members of the service of one republic to be present in another republic. In the event that they could not agree, the two republics, we would then interfere as mediators for coming into contact and do the internal affairs work if we assessed that it was necessary for us to interfere.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: The Prosecution now plays another short clip and it's actually already admitted. Exhibit P12. It is a short clip of a celebration of the Krajina Security Service Day on 5 July 1993. And for the booth, it's clip 4.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "On this day, three years ago, the first large gathering of people and mass protests against the Croatian leadership took place in Knin. The result of those events was a petition signed by the policemen of the then Knin public security station refusing obedience to the pro-Ustasha authorities in Zagreb and refusing to wear markings worn by Ustashas 50 years ago while committing genocide against the Serbian people. The central celebration took place in Knin. Milan Martic, minister of the interior, spoke at the formal events, stressing at the end of his speech that the chequer-board flag can be in Knin only 'over our dead bodies.' Among other speakers addressing the gathering were Goran Hadzic, president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and Milan Babic, president of the Knin Municipal Assembly. On the occasion of the Day of Security of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, there were issued the 'Serbian rebellions and uprisings' decorations, medals for courage, and certificates of gratitude issued, among others, to Belgrade Radio and Television and the 'Vecernje Novosti' daily."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hoffmann, if you leave your microphone open then we'll follow all your conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: I'm just looking at the transcript which may have not caught up all the transcript, as it looks now. I'm wondering if we have to replay the clip. The Court Reporter is shaking her head, so I think I can continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if the interpreters have had no problems either, then we can continue. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Witness, did you recognise any of the people attending the celebration on the clip that you just saw?

utterances.speaker: JF-038
utterances.text: Well, yes, I did. I recognise Mr. Stanisic, Milan Martic, Goran Hadzic. As for the others, I don't remember them anymore. I probably met them in the field, but I can't really be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: I'll ask that 65 ter 4719 be brought up on the screen. The ERN starts with 0414-2989.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And this is a list of people being awarded by the RSK on the Security Service Day, July 5. And my question to you is if -- having reviewed this document earlier on, if you recognise any names on this list? And we can start with page -- it's only one page in the original.

utterances.speaker: JF-038
utterances.text: I tend to remember persons rather than names, so I couldn't really put together based on the photos and the names here except for Jovica Stanisic here under number 1 on the list, and he is present. The other person, Nebojsa Pavkovic, was not in that video-clip. I don't really know the next name but I can't really put the names and tie them or link them to the picture, the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Just one more question. If you could look at person listed under number 20.

utterances.speaker: JF-038
utterances.text: Yes, it says there "Dragan Vasiljkovic - Captain Dragan."

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution tenders this exhibit into evidence, which is 65 ter 4719.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 4719 becomes Exhibit P428, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P428 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Witness, you testified previously how you met in Knin also with General Ratko Mladic. And during cross-examination in Martic, that is at transcript 3135, you were asked about the KOS. And I just have a short question, if you can explain what KOS stands for?

utterances.speaker: JF-038
utterances.text: That's the counter-intelligence service, counter-intelligence service of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Was that abbreviation, KOS, used at that time, that is, in 1991?

utterances.speaker: JF-038
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm now turning to the area of Slavonia and Baranja, the so-called SAO SBWS. And just for your orientation the relevant map in the Court binder would be map 18, already admitted as Exhibit P9.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Witness, you briefly indicated already in your Martic testimony that in mid-August 1991, you were sent on a similar mission, this time to the area of Osijek and finally to Beli Manastir in the SAO SBWS. And my question to you, during that mission to the area of Slavonia and Baranja, did you learn anything about the presence of any paramilitary unit in that area, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JF-038
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Could you please list any such paramilitary unit, and if you know the respective commander of such units?

utterances.speaker: JF-038
utterances.text: Since I was tasked by my superior as the leader of the group for Osijek to try and verify the situation in Srem and Osijek, I went together with a security man, a police officer who was armed, and in the presence of a security officer, a military security officer who was in charge of that area, together we visited some of the villages near Manastir and in the town itself. A lot of people had moved out of that area and those who remained were mostly the elderly who could not leave their homes. And in our interviews with them, they told us about their problems, that they were afraid because of the presence of some paramilitary units and most of them mentioned and complained about Beli Orlovi, the paramilitary units of Vuk Draskovic, but they probably did not differentiate. They talked about units generally, but the Beli Orlovi, White Eagles and whatnot. So they mentioned also the people, Giska Beli. They also talked about the presence of Chetniks, Chetnik detachments, about Badza's Group or groups, also about the presence of the Frenki's Men, the Red Berets, Badza's Group, so-called, Stojkovic's group. They mentioned some special MUP units and that was it. But most of these people were elderly people, so they couldn't really make a distinction, but I heard from them the problems that they were facing and the people that they encountered. One day, when I was in the barracks in Beli Manastir, the barracks commander, if you want me I can mention his name, but then we would have to go to closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: In fact, let me take you back just to the groups that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me, I have a comment to make or, rather, an objection, but I would like to say my objection in the -- not in the presence of this witness. I will be very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and you want to say it in your own language so we have to invite the witness to leave the courtroom, or?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I can try to do it in English but I would like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but then, of course, first we would have to inquire whether -- Witness JF-038, do you understand the English language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please take your earphones off. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is the notification issue about the essence of charges against my client. Now the witness mentioned for the very first time, as far as I know, the presence of my client's men or something like that in the area of Baranja. We have his statement, we had his testimony in Martic case, we had a proofing note which was done -- which was done yesterday, and there is -- something like that is not mentioned in any of these instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Can I just briefly respond directly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's first allow Mr. Petrovic to finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Just if I can add something more. I can't believe that it is possible that my learned colleague had not asked the question about one of the accused before this Chamber. I'm sure that he put that question. I would be surprised if he did not. And I did not find any evidence that anything which has any connection with my client was to be expected with this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, perhaps before you respond, anything to add, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I anticipate -- I do join in the objection. I anticipate what my learned friend will say is that the subject was dealt with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's not speculate on what your learned friend --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's not so much speculate. There is notice of a kind in a previous transcript which relates to when the witness gave evidence previously, but the Prosecution have not included that transcript in their Rule 92 ter application. They have not included it in any proofing note. So by virtue of that, the Defence were effectively told, This is not evidence we are going to lead. Therefore, we have not concerned ourselves with it. Now my learned friend is seeking to go behind that notification, simply lead the evidence without providing any notice to the Defence as to what the witness will say, and I endorse what my learned friend has said. Mr. Hoffmann must have discussed this with the witness during the proofing sessions and has simply decided not to deal with it by disclosing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you have already responded to what you expected Mr. Hoffmann would say. Let's first verify whether that's his position. Mr. Hoffmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Yeah, I'd tried to cut this discussion very short. There was an earlier proofing session many years ago and an information report was filed on 11 February 2008 which in detail outlines that part, and it's at paragraphs 16 following. In that proofing note it covers the mission to the SBWS and it mentions all the groups that he just mentioned. Plus I think it is part -- there is no need for a further notice if this witness already testified about the same issues in this very trial, in the first round of trial, so to say, but I would not expect that -- apart from that, we gave them notice in 2008, early 2008, that is, two years ago, that if this witness gave evidence when this trial started the first time, that we then, in addition, have to notify the Defence he may give evidence to the same effect that he did the first time. I'm, to be honest, a bit surprised by that objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have to verify all these reference to earlier proofing notes. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can add, I'm not aware of any proofing note from 2008.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That raises the issue as to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Maybe it goes to the situation our Defence team is in, but I simply do not -- that's not disclosed to -- as far as I know, I never find that. And there is not a single reference in all materials, 65 ter materials or weekly notifications, nothing refers to a proofing note of 2008. I have never seen it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's take it step by step. The Chamber, of course, has no access to all the material which is available. I just refer to one thing I noticed, that is that in the Martic testimony, the witness was asked about a statement given at an earlier stage, which was not tendered into evidence, is not -- at least is not tendered in this case. We only have the -- unless there's any question about that, but we have only the three transcripts of the Martic case in which reference is made to other statements which we do not have. So, therefore, the Chamber is not in every respect fully aware of what the witness may have said before and whether that was disclosed, yes or no. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: If you allow me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: -- just to give a brief reference to the earlier testimony in this very case two years ago, and that is on 6 May 2008, on transcript 1119, following. He's specifically asked about paramilitary units and he mentions Badza's Group, Frenki's Men, Frenki Simatovic, Arkan's Men. It has been raised already in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Mr. Stanisic was then assisted by -- was represented by Mr. Knoops?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, he was. But the point is a different one. Of course, I accept --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you say, how could we possibly understand that this would be the subject of -- so there -- at least at that time in the presence of Mr. Knoops, these matters were raised and that was available. So even if it's not in a statement, at least it is on a transcript of that date. Not to say whatever conclusions to be drawn out of that, but I just want to first establish what has happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. We accept that it is in the transcript, that transcript and we accept there is mention of Frenki's Men in a proofing note of the 11th February 2008. Neither of those things were subject to the Rule 92 ter application. That is what we took as the notice of what this witness would testify about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may quickly respond on this matter. I think it hasn't been a practice in any case, if a witness has given a prior statement or a prior testimony that has been disclosed to the Defence, that the Prosecution is asked to provide a proofing note summarising again what is already in statements or -- and it has been practice in this case that we haven't tendered normally all the statements of witnesses but still led evidence on what the witness have testified prior. It's obvious with witnesses who testify viva voce. We are leading evidence that they have given in prior statements, still they are not part of any 92 ter package, but nobody requires then to -- us to provide additional summary of a statement that is already disclosed to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we have two matters. The first is disclosure, and the second is notice of what evidence will be elicited from a witness. Let's be clear, sometimes you can disclose statements which you might not consider to elicit the evidence or all of the evidence of the statements disclosed. Now, it seems that we are at a crossroads here because the Defence is aware of previous testimony given and, if I understand you well, now claims how could we expect that this is now to be elicited again because it has not been mentioned after that. So we are more or less in a grey zone between disclosure and notice given of the expected evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: If you would allow me just on that notice issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: The Defence has just a few moments stated that they would clearly have expected me to ask those questions about the accused. Now being aware that this witness did talk about Frenki's Men before, how could they not expect me to ask about the same evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, the simple answer is because the 92 ter notice didn't include it, and the 92 ter notice is what we have as our road map as to what the Prosecution are going to have a witness testify to. Or else we will just have to search through hundreds of pages of transcripts and guess at what the Prosecution might want to testify or might want a witness to testify to, additional to that which they've notified in the Rule 92 ter application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does the matter appear in your 65 ter summary, Mr. Hoffmann?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: I do think so that it in general terms appears in the 65 ter summary, and then, of course, it's a matter that has been notified to the Defence by the proofing notes and by his prior testimony. And if I may respond on the 92 ter argument, 92 ter means that we are tendering something in writing. So obviously, part of the 92 ter application is the part that we are not dealing explicitly in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but then --

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: So we don't give normally an outline of -- and we have never been asked to give an outline of the areas that we cover. That would be new to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least if that outline is to be found elsewhere because 92 ter is not meant to keep away from the Defence the notice which is usually given under 65 ter.
